I can’t quote the “current” California statute or say whether your checkout flow complies because (a) I don’t have browsing or legal-database access right now and (b) my training data only goes through June 2024. For questions about law that may have changed since then, I must rely on you providing the current text or allow me to fetch it — otherwise I can’t reliably cite or quote the controlling statute.

What I can do now
- Explain what the California Automatic Renewal Law (ARL) required as of mid‑2024 (clearly labeled as possibly outdated).  
- Give a practical checklist you can use to compare your checkout flow against typical ARL requirements.  
- If you paste the exact checkout copy/flow you use (buttons, disclosures, confirmation email text, cancellation steps), I can map those items to the checklist and flag likely issues (but not give a binding legal determination).  
- Tell you where to look to get the authoritative, up‑to‑date statute text and official guidance.

Brief background (may be outdated)
- As of my last update (June 2024), California’s Automatic Renewal Law was commonly found in the California Business and Professions Code (often cited as §17600 et seq.) and required that businesses using automatic renewals or negative‑option subscriptions: clear and conspicuous disclosure of the automatic renewal terms before purchase; affirmative consent to those terms; and a post‑purchase acknowledgement (receipt) that includes the renewal and cancellation terms and a description of how to cancel. The law also imposed requirements about the ease of cancellation and additional protections for free trials that roll into paid subscriptions. (This summary is not a quote and may not reflect changes after June 2024.)

Practical checklist to evaluate your checkout flow
Compare your flow against each item below. If any are missing or unclear, that’s a likely compliance risk under ARL‑style rules:

1. Pre‑purchase disclosure (clear & conspicuous)
  - Before the consumer completes checkout, do you clearly disclose: that the purchase will automatically renew (or is a negative option), the recurring charge amount, billing frequency, and any trial-to-paid transition?
  - Is this disclosure visually prominent (not buried in long terms), and plain language?

2. Affirmative consent
  - Does the consumer affirmatively agree to the automatic renewal terms (e.g., an unchecked checkbox they must check, or an explicit “I agree” that references the renewal terms) prior to charging?

3. Post‑purchase confirmation/acknowledgment
  - After purchase, do you send a confirmation (email or immediately visible page) that restates the key renewal terms and provides the cancellation method/instructions?

4. Easy cancellation mechanism
  - Is there a cancellation method that is as easy (or easier) than subscribing — e.g., online through account settings, a single click, or the same channel used to subscribe? Are the steps described clearly?
  - If cancellation requires contacting customer service, is the process straightforward and spelled out?

5. Material changes and renewal reminders
  - For material changes to the subscription terms (price, billing frequency, etc.), do you obtain consent or provide notice per applicable rules?
  - If required by statute or regulation, do you send a reminder before renewal (some laws require a reminder for certain renewals; check current statute)?

6. Free trial rules (if applicable)
  - If you offer a free trial that converts to paid, did you disclose trial length, the fact that it converts to paid, the dollar amount that will be charged, and how to cancel to avoid charges?

7. Recordkeeping & internal proof
  - Can you demonstrate where, when, and how the consumer was presented the disclosure and gave consent (timestamps, screenshots, server logs)?

8. Pricing clarity & renewal charges
  - Are any auto‑renewed fees clearly itemized (taxes, shipping, additional fees) so consumer knows exact amount to be charged?

How I can help immediately (without browsing)
- If you paste the checkout screen
